title: Operators & Expressions
summary: **Operators** combine values into **expressions** that evaluate to a single result. Go keeps this deliberately small and predictable: a handful of arithmetic, comparison, logical, and bitwise operators, just **five precedence levels**, **no implicit numeric conversions**, and — surprisingly — `++` and `--` are **statements, not expressions**.

subtopics.title: Arithmetic & the % rules
subtopics.explanation: + - * / % work on numbers. Integer division truncates toward zero (7/2 == 3), while float division is exact-ish (7.0/2 == 3.5). The remainder operator % is only defined for integers, and its sign follows the dividend.

subtopics.title: Integer overflow wraps around
subtopics.explanation: Fixed-width integers don't error on overflow — they wrap modulo 2^bits. An int8 maxes at 127; adding 1 wraps to -128. This is defined behavior in Go, not undefined as in C.

subtopics.title: Logical operators short-circuit
subtopics.explanation: && and || evaluate left-to-right and stop as soon as the result is known: false && x never evaluates x, and true || y never evaluates y. This lets you guard against nil or division by zero in one expression.
subtopics.example: if p != nil && p.ok { ... } // safe: p.ok only read if p != nil

subtopics.title: Bitwise operators incl. &^ (AND NOT)
subtopics.explanation: & | ^ operate bit-by-bit; << and >> shift. Go's unique &^ is 'bit clear' (AND NOT): a &^ b clears in a every bit set in b. As a unary operator, ^x is bitwise complement (Go has no ~).

subtopics.title: No implicit conversions
subtopics.explanation: Go never silently mixes numeric types. You cannot add an int to a float64 — you must convert explicitly with T(x). This prevents a whole class of precision and sign bugs.
subtopics.example:
var i int = 3
var f float64 = 2.5
_ = float64(i) + f // must convert i

subtopics.title: Precedence & ++/-- are statements
subtopics.explanation: Go collapses C's many precedence levels into just five (highest: * / % << >> & &^, then + - | ^, then comparisons, then &&, then ||). Crucially, ++ and -- are statements: you cannot write b = a++ or use them inside an expression.
subtopics.example:
x := 2 + 3*4   // 14, * binds tighter
i++            // statement only — never `j = i++`

foundations.overview: Almost every line of Go computes something from existing values: adding sizes, comparing keys, masking flags, guarding a nil pointer. Operators are the verbs that do this, and an expression is any combination of operands and operators that produces a value. Go's design philosophy of 'less is more' shows clearly here — fewer operators, fewer precedence levels, and no hidden type coercion, so an expression means exactly what it looks like.
foundations.formalDefinition: An expression specifies the computation of a value by applying operators to operands. Operators are symbols (unary or binary) with a fixed precedence and left-associativity that combine typed operands of compatible types into a single typed result.
foundations.whyItMatters: Misreading precedence, forgetting integer truncation, or assuming implicit conversion are among the most common beginner bugs and a frequent interview topic. Understanding short-circuit evaluation also enables safe, idiomatic guard expressions.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of an expression as a small tree: operators are nodes, operands are leaves, and Go evaluates from the leaves up using precedence to decide which node binds first. Parentheses just reshape the tree.
foundations.runtimePerspective: The compiler folds constant expressions at compile time (untyped constants have arbitrary precision), checks that operand types match exactly, and emits machine instructions for the rest. Integer arithmetic compiles to native CPU ops that wrap on overflow; there is no runtime type promotion.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Computing buffer offsets, packing/unpacking flag bitmasks, paginating with division and modulo, comparing version numbers, and guarding optional values with short-circuit logic.
foundations.businessImpact: Correct operator usage prevents silent data corruption (overflow, truncation) that can manifest as wrong invoices, miscounted inventory, or security flaws — bugs that are expensive to find in production.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Explicit conversions and a tiny precedence table make code reviews faster and expressions unambiguous, lowering the cognitive load of reading unfamiliar Go.
foundations.performanceImpact: Bitwise ops and shifts are single-cycle and used for fast multiply/divide by powers of two and compact flag storage. Short-circuit evaluation also skips expensive right-hand operands when the result is already determined.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Dividing two ints can give a fraction (5/2 == 2.5).
commonMisconceptions.reality: Integer division truncates toward zero, so 5/2 == 2. Convert an operand to float first: float64(5)/2 == 2.5.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Integer overflow crashes or is undefined like in C.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Go defines overflow as wrapping modulo 2^bits. It's deterministic but still usually a bug to watch for.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can write `b = a++` like in C.
commonMisconceptions.reality: In Go, ++ and -- are statements, not expressions. They produce no value and can't appear inside another expression.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Go promotes int to float64 automatically when you mix them.
commonMisconceptions.reality: There are no implicit numeric conversions. Mixing typed int and float64 is a compile error; you must convert explicitly with float64(x).

visualExplorer.title: How Go evaluates `2 + 3*4 > 10 && ok`
visualExplorer.caption: Precedence and short-circuit decide the order — not left-to-right reading.

config.intro: Evaluating the expression `2 + 3*4 > 10 && ok` step by step:

steps.name: Highest: * / % << >> & &^
steps.detail: `3*4` binds tightest and evaluates first, giving `2 + 12 > 10 && ok`.

steps.name: Next: + - | ^
steps.detail: Addition runs next: `2 + 12` is `14`, leaving `14 > 10 && ok`.

steps.name: Then comparisons
steps.detail: `14 > 10` evaluates to the bool `true`, leaving `true && ok`.

steps.name: Then && (short-circuit)
steps.detail: Because the left side is `true`, Go must look at `ok`; if it were `false`, `ok` would be skipped entirely.

steps.name: Finally || (lowest)
steps.detail: There is no `||` here, so the `&&` result is the value of the whole expression — a single bool.

interactiveExamples.title: Integer vs float division and remainder
interactiveExamples.explanation: Integer division truncates; you must convert to float64 to keep the fraction. % gives the remainder and takes the sign of the dividend.

code.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	a, b := 7, 2
	fmt.Println(a / b)              // 3  — integer division truncates
	fmt.Println(a % b)              // 1  — remainder
	fmt.Println(float64(a) / float64(b)) // 3.5 — explicit float conversion
	fmt.Println(-7 % 3)            // -1 — sign follows the dividend
}

checkpoints.explanation: * binds tighter than +, so 2 + 3*4 == 14. Integer division 10/3 truncates to 3, and 10 % 3 is the remainder 1.

checkpoints.prompt: Which statement about Go's ++ operator is correct?
options: ++ returns the old value, so j becomes 0
++ returns the new value, so j becomes 1
++ is a statement, not an expression, so `j := i++` does not compile
++ is only allowed inside for loops
checkpoints.explanation: In Go, ++ and -- are statements that produce no value. You cannot use them inside an expression, so `j := i++` is a compile error. Use i++ on its own line, then assign i.

result := i * f
fmt.Println(result)
options: Go has no implicit numeric conversion, so int and float64 can't be mixed; convert with float64(i)
result must be declared with var

checkpoints.explanation: Go never auto-promotes between numeric types. `i * f` mixes int and float64, which is a compile error ('invalid operation: mismatched types'). Convert explicitly: float64(i) * f.

checkpoints.prompt: Clear the Write bit from perm while leaving the others untouched.
checkpoints.codeBefore:
perm := Read | Write | Exec
perm = perm
checkpoints.explanation: &^ is Go's AND NOT (bit clear) operator: it clears in perm exactly the bits set in Write. ^ would toggle Write, | would set it, and & would keep only Write.

codeLab.title: Detect a power of two with bitwise tricks
codeLab.instructions: Implement `IsPowerOfTwo(n int) bool` that returns true when n is a positive power of two (1, 2, 4, 8, ...). Use the classic bit trick rather than a loop: a power of two has exactly one bit set, so n & (n-1) == 0.
hints: A power of two in binary is a single 1 followed by zeros: 0b100, 0b1000.
Subtracting 1 flips that bit to 0 and all lower bits to 1, so n & (n-1) clears the only set bit.
Guard with n > 0 first, because && short-circuits and 0 and negatives are not powers of two.

debuggingLab.title: Percentage always prints 0

brokenCode.caption: The conversion happens too late.

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: hits / total is integer division: 3 / 4 truncates to 0, and only then is 0 converted to float64(0) == 0.0. The float64 conversion is applied to the already-truncated integer result, so the fraction is lost before it ever becomes a float.
commonMistakes: Converting the result of integer division instead of an operand.
Assuming / picks float division automatically when the destination is float64.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Convert at least one operand to float64 BEFORE the division so Go performs float division.

theory.question: What is short-circuit evaluation, and how do && and || use it in Go?
theory.directAnswer: Short-circuit evaluation means a logical operator stops as soon as the result is determined. `false && x` returns false without evaluating x, and `true || y` returns true without evaluating y. Go evaluates the operands strictly left to right, so the right-hand side may never run.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A guarantee that && and || only evaluate their right operand when it can still affect the result.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: It enables concise guard expressions (e.g. check a pointer is non-nil before dereferencing) and avoids unnecessary or unsafe work.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: && returns false immediately if the left operand is false; || returns true immediately if the left operand is true. Otherwise the right operand is evaluated and returned.

theory.whyImportant: It is the idiomatic way to write nil and bounds guards safely, and a common interview probe about evaluation order and side effects.
theory.realWorldExample: `if user != nil && user.IsAdmin()` never calls IsAdmin on a nil pointer because && short-circuits.

followUps.question: Do bitwise & and | short-circuit?
followUps.answer: No. & and | always evaluate both operands; only the logical && and || short-circuit.

followUps.question: Can short-circuiting change program behavior beyond performance?
followUps.answer: Yes — if the right operand has side effects (a function call, a panic-prone access), short-circuiting decides whether they happen.

theory.question: Why does Go require explicit numeric conversions, and what does &^ do?
theory.directAnswer: Go has no implicit numeric conversions: you cannot combine, say, an int and a float64 in one expression without an explicit T(x) conversion, which prevents silent precision and sign bugs. The &^ operator is 'AND NOT' (bit clear): a &^ b clears in a every bit that is set in b.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two of Go's deliberate simplifications: mandatory explicit conversions and a dedicated bit-clear operator.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Explicitness makes type-mixing visible at the call site; &^ removes the need for the common `a & ^b` idiom and reads clearly as 'clear these bits'.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Mixed-type arithmetic is a compile error until you wrap an operand in its target type. a &^ b is equivalent to a & (^b) but is a single, clearer operator.

theory.whyImportant: Both are uniquely Go and frequently tested; misunderstanding them causes compile errors or subtle flag-handling bugs.
theory.realWorldExample: Clearing a permission bit: perm = perm &^ Write removes write access while leaving read and exec intact.

followUps.question: Does Go have a ~ (bitwise NOT) operator?
followUps.answer: No. Go uses unary ^ for bitwise complement: ^x flips all bits, so ^0 is -1 for a signed int.

followUps.question: What happens on int8(200)?
followUps.answer: It is a constant overflow error at compile time; converting a runtime int that's out of range simply wraps modulo 256.

scenario.question: A counter stored in an int32 occasionally jumps from a large positive value to a large negative one in production. What's happening and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: The counter is overflowing. int32 maxes at 2,147,483,647; the next increment wraps to -2,147,483,648 because Go defines integer overflow as wrapping modulo 2^bits rather than erroring. Fix it by using a wider type (int64 or uint64), checking before incrementing, or using atomic counters sized appropriately.

detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Hardware integers are fixed width; Go chooses defined two's-complement wrapping for portability and speed rather than C's undefined behavior.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Adding past the maximum representable value carries past the sign bit, flipping the value to the most negative number.

scenario.whyImportant: Silent wraparound corrupts counters, IDs, and offsets in long-running services and is a classic production incident.
scenario.realWorldExample: A monotonically increasing request-ID counter using int32 wraps after ~2.1 billion requests, colliding with old IDs.

followUps.question: How can you detect overflow before it happens?
followUps.answer: Compare against the type's max (math.MaxInt32) before adding, or use math/bits / checked arithmetic helpers.

followUps.question: Does unsigned arithmetic also wrap?
followUps.answer: Yes, uint types wrap modulo 2^bits too; a uint that goes below 0 wraps to a huge positive value.

coding.question: Implement `func CountSetBits(n uint) int` that returns the number of 1 bits in n (population count), using bitwise operators.
coding.thoughtProcess: Use Brian Kernighan's trick: n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit each iteration, so the loop runs once per set bit instead of once per total bit. Count the iterations until n becomes 0.
coding.lineByLine: Each pass, n & (n-1) turns off the rightmost 1 bit, so the loop body runs exactly once for every set bit. We increment count per cleared bit and stop when n reaches 0, returning the total number of 1 bits.
coding.timeComplexity: O(k) where k is the number of set bits (at most the bit width)

followUps.question: Is there a standard-library way?
followUps.answer: Yes — bits.OnesCount(n) from math/bits is the idiomatic, often hardware-accelerated choice.

followUps.question: Why use n & (n-1) instead of shifting and checking each bit?
followUps.answer: It only iterates per set bit, so it's faster for sparse values than scanning all bits.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Model permission and feature sets as bitmask flags (iota with 1<<n) so you can combine, test, and clear capabilities with | & &^ in a single int — compact to store and cheap to compare.
productionDeepDive.performance: Prefer shifts (x<<3) and masks (x & 0xFF) over multiply/divide and modulo where applicable; they are single-cycle. Rely on && short-circuiting to skip expensive validation when an early condition already fails.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Read-modify-write on a shared counter (c++ or c |= flag) is not atomic; multiple goroutines will lose updates. Use sync/atomic or a mutex for shared integer state.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Guard against integer overflow on counters and offsets in long-running services by sizing types generously (int64) or validating before arithmetic; remember overflow wraps silently rather than panicking.
productionDeepDive.observability: When debugging flag logic, print integers with %b or %03b to see the actual bit pattern, and assert expected masks in tests so a wrong operator (^ vs &^) is caught early.
productionDeepDive.security: Avoid mixing signed and unsigned in size/length math: a negative int converted to uint becomes huge and can defeat bounds checks. Always validate ranges before converting, especially for values from untrusted input.

caseStudies.problem: A 32-bit monotonic counter silently wrapped after ~2.1B events, causing duplicate IDs.
caseStudies.solution: Migrated counters to int64/uint64 and added a pre-increment overflow check.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Slightly larger storage and wire size for far higher headroom.
caseStudies.lessons: Integer overflow in Go is defined (wraps) but still a latent correctness bug — size integer types for the full expected lifetime.

keyTakeaways: Integer division truncates and % is integer-only; convert an operand to float64 explicitly for fractional results.
&& and || short-circuit left-to-right — ideal for nil and bounds guards — while bitwise & | always evaluate both sides.
Go's bitwise set includes &^ (AND NOT / bit clear) and uses unary ^ for complement; there is no ~.
There are no implicit numeric conversions, integer overflow wraps modulo 2^bits, and ++/-- are statements, not expressions.
Go has only five precedence levels (highest: * / % << >> & &^), so when in doubt, add parentheses for clarity.
